title: As the Word comes to me, Lalo
hook: as the Lord's Word comes to me, so I speak, Lalo (Tilang M1, ang 722)
tomorrow: The one whose head He guards

segments.voice: Yesterday, thaakur, master, and your line: ask your master. Today the asking stops, and Guru Nanak speaks hard truth to an old friend.

A town is sacked. Tradition says Guru Nanak was there, at Saidpur, when Babur's army came down from Kabul, and that he was taken captive for a time. Early in the path, we met this town's carpenter, Bhai Lalo, whose plain bread Guru Nanak chose over a rich man's feast. Afterward, Guru Nanak sang about what he'd seen. And he addressed the song not to a king, and not to the crowd, but to his friend, the carpenter.
screen: `THE SAME TOWN IS SACKED.` → `LALO, THE CARPENTER OF SAIDPUR.` → `A SONG TO A FRIEND.`

segments.voice: The shabad is in Raag Tilang, on ang 722. It opens, in effect: as the Master's Word comes to me, so I speak, Lalo. Then it describes the invasion with terrible clarity. The invader came from Kabul like a wedding party of sin, demanding a bride by force. Modesty and righteousness hid themselves; falsehood strutted about as leader. The religious officials of both communities, the qazis and the brahmins, were pushed aside. And the women, the hymn says, women of every community, suffered. Songs of blood were being sung. Two things stand out. First, the courage. Guru Nanak names an invader's violence plainly, while that power was rising over Punjab. He doesn't soften it or flatter it. Second, why he can. The first line is the key: as the Word comes to me, so I speak. The word is baani, the same word that's in Gurbani, the Guru's word. Guru Nanak isn't offering his own opinion about politics. He's saying the Word moves through him, and he won't edit it to keep himself safe. The line is often quoted as a standard for honest speech: say what is true, as it comes, even to power. And notice who hears it first. Not the emperor's court. Lalo, a working man, a friend who lived under that power. The shabad can be heard as grief, as protest, and as a sign that the Word would not stay silent.
screen: `AS THE WORD COMES, SO I SPEAK.` · `A WEDDING PARTY OF SIN FROM KABUL.` · `SONGS OF BLOOD, PLAINLY NAMED.` · `TOLD FIRST TO A WORKING FRIEND.` · then, large: `AS THE WORD COMES.`

segments.voice: Think of something true you've been holding back, at work, in your family, with a friend: not a cruel truth or a rant, but a true one, said with care. Notice whether you've been editing it to keep yourself safe, and picture saying it plainly, as it comes, to the right person. If you pray, ask the One for courage with a quiet Waheguru.
Baani, the Word, speech from the Master: Guru Nanak to Bhai Lalo, as it comes to me, so I speak, even about an invader's violence.
Your line: as the word comes. Plain speech doesn't have to be cruel. Six hundred fifty-nine days in.

howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Nanak's Tilang shabad addressed to Bhai Lalo, one of the hymns known as the Babar Vani, and cite its opening line as a model of fearless, truthful speech.

original.note: Gurmukhi: the Word, speech from the Master; khasam kee baanee, the Master's Word.

trapdoor: what you thought: Guru Nanak commenting on the news.
what it means: the Word speaking through him, unedited, even about an invading king.

what a scholar hears: the Tilang shabad is one of the Babar Vani hymns on Babur's invasions, which tradition holds Guru Nanak witnessed; its opening line grounds prophetic speech in baani rather than personal opinion.

chat.says: Did Guru Nanak ever speak out about the violence of his own day?
options: Yes, he named an invader's cruelty plainly: as the Word comes to me, so I speak.
No, he kept his hymns to inner peace and never mentioned rulers or wars.
Yes, but only years later, once the invader was gone and it was safe.
chat.meaning: In the Tilang shabad Guru Nanak tells Lalo, as the Master's Word comes to me, so I speak, and names the invasion's violence plainly.

notes: Sensitive: the hymn describes violence against women; the script names it without detail. Confirm the handling.
Confirm the date (around 1521) and the tradition that Guru Nanak was taken captive at Saidpur.
Paraphrase covers 'paap kee janj lai kaabaloh dhaaiaa', 'saram dharam doe chhap khaloe, koorr phirai pardhaan', the qazis and brahmins set aside, and 'khoon ke sohile gaaveeah'; confirm.
Babur's faith is not mentioned, to avoid making a tradition the foil; the hymn itself sets aside officials of both communities.
